title: THE BIBLE DIDN’T HIDE THE SEXUAL SCANDALS, BETRAYALS, AND BROKEN MARRIAGES—BECAUSE JESUS CAME TO SAVE THE PEOPLE WE THOUGHT WERE BEYOND REDEMPTION
paragraphs: THE BIBLE DIDN’T HIDE THE SEXUAL SCANDALS, BETRAYALS, AND BROKEN MARRIAGES—BECAUSE JESUS CAME TO SAVE THE PEOPLE WE THOUGHT WERE BEYOND REDEMPTION

Incest. Exploitation. Adultery. Polygamy. False accusations. Shattered families. Scripture exposes what humanity tries to bury—but behind its darkest stories stands a Savior whose grace is greater than our shame, whose holiness confronts our sin, and whose mercy can rewrite even the most devastating chapters of a human life.
“And such were some of you: but ye are washed, but ye are sanctified, but ye are justified in the name of the Lord Jesus, and by the Spirit of our God.” — 1 Corinthians 6:11 (KJV)
There are stories in the Bible that would make an entire church congregation fall silent if they happened today.
A father intoxicated by his own daughters.
A woman sexually exploited by the very men who should have protected her.
A king who took another man's wife and arranged her husband's death.
A family torn apart by multiple wives, jealousy, favoritism, and wounded children.
A faithful young man falsely accused of sexual assault because he refused to surrender his integrity.
And a woman dragged before a crowd, her sin exposed, while the people holding stones seemed completely uninterested in examining their own hearts.
These aren't stories from some scandalous novel.
They're in the Bible.
And perhaps the most uncomfortable question isn't why God allowed these stories to be recorded.
Perhaps it's why we keep pretending the people sitting beside us in church don't carry stories just as complicated.
Because somewhere, a woman is worshiping with a heart still bleeding from betrayal.
A husband is smiling for the family photograph while his marriage is quietly falling apart.
A young believer is drowning in sexual shame, wondering whether God is already tired of forgiving them.
Someone who was exploited years ago still believes the terrible lie that what happened to them made them dirty.
And someone who committed a serious sin is sitting alone tonight, convinced that the worst thing they ever did has become the only thing God will ever see.
If any of those people sound familiar, please keep reading.
Because the Bible doesn't merely reveal what human beings have done.
It reveals what Jesus Christ can do with human beings who desperately need redemption.
But we must begin with a truth that modern Christianity sometimes struggles to hold together.
God's grace is astonishing.
And God's holiness is not negotiable.
Grace does not rename evil as good. Forgiveness does not erase accountability. Restoration does not require victims to return to unsafe relationships.
And the Gospel never asks someone who has been abused to carry the guilt of the person who abused them.
That distinction matters more than many people realize.
Consider Lot's family.
Genesis 19:30–38 records a deeply disturbing account in which Lot's daughters intoxicated their father and had sexual relations with him while he was unaware of what was happening.
Scripture records the event without celebrating it.
It does not present their conduct as a model of faithfulness or marriage.
The account exposes a family in moral and spiritual collapse, where fear, isolation, intoxication, and grievously distorted judgment lead to incest.
There is no need to soften what happened.
There is also no need to invent a lesson the passage never teaches.
The Bible's willingness to record a sin is not God's permission to commit it.
In fact, Leviticus 18 explicitly prohibits incestuous sexual relationships.
And if someone reading this has suffered sexual abuse within their own family, hear this carefully.
You were not responsible for another person's violation of your body.
You do not become guilty because someone else chose to sin against you.
Your dignity was not destroyed by what was done to you.
The Lord who sees what people hide does not confuse the wounded with the one who inflicted the wound.
Sometimes the first step toward healing isn't confessing a sin.
Sometimes it's finally understanding that you were sinned against.
And Jesus cares about that distinction.
Then there is Tamar.
Not every Tamar in Scripture has the same story.

In Genesis 38, Judah's daughter-in-law Tamar was denied the family provision associated with her widowhood. After Judah failed to fulfill his responsibility, she disguised herself, and Judah unknowingly had sexual relations with her.
The story is morally complicated. It does not establish deception or sexual wrongdoing as righteous methods.
But it does reveal something deeply uncomfortable about human hypocrisy.
When Tamar's pregnancy became known, Judah was ready to condemn her.
Then the evidence exposed his own involvement.
And Judah confessed:
“She hath been more righteous than I.” — Genesis 38:26 (KJV)
Imagine that moment.
A man prepared to pronounce judgment suddenly confronted by the truth about himself.
How many times have we seen something similar?
A person publicly condemns a sin while privately protecting a secret.
A leader demands accountability from others but refuses to accept it personally.
A family protects its reputation while ignoring the suffering of its most vulnerable members.
And sometimes the loudest accusation in the room is coming from someone terrified that their own wrongdoing might be discovered.
Yet Tamar's story contains another astonishing detail.
Matthew 1:3 includes Tamar in the genealogy of Jesus Christ.
Not because everything in her story was good.
Not because every human decision was righteous.
But because God's redemptive purposes were not defeated by human brokenness.
The family history leading to the Messiah was not edited to make humanity look respectable.
Then consider another Tamar, the daughter of King David.
Her story in 2 Samuel 13 is devastating.
Her half-brother Amnon became consumed with desire for her. He manipulated circumstances, overpowered her, and sexually assaulted her despite her protests.
Afterward, he rejected her.
And Tamar was left devastated.
Scripture does not portray her suffering as a romantic misunderstanding.
It shows violence, violation, humiliation, and the terrible consequences of unchecked evil within a powerful family.
For anyone who has endured sexual violence, Tamar's story is a reminder that Scripture does not require survivors to pretend that their suffering was insignificant.
Her pain mattered.
Her protest mattered.
The injustice mattered.
And the failure of those around her to respond rightly mattered.
There are wounds that cannot be healed by telling someone to stop thinking about what happened.
There are violations that require protection, truth, justice, compassionate care, and time.
God's power to restore does not mean every relationship should be restored.
Sometimes the most faithful response to evil is to expose it, protect the vulnerable, and refuse to give an abuser another opportunity to harm.
Forgiveness must never become a religious disguise for enabling abuse.
Now look at David.
The shepherd boy.
The worshiper.
The warrior.
The king.
The man who wrote psalms that still bring comfort to suffering souls.
And yet, in 2 Samuel 11, David took Bathsheba, another man's wife, and afterward arranged for her husband Uriah to be killed.
The passage describes a king wielding enormous power. It would be irresponsible to ignore the power imbalance between David and Bathsheba or to assume she freely shared his guilt.
The narrative places the responsibility for these royal abuses squarely upon David.
And God did not excuse him because he was anointed.
God sent Nathan.
The prophet confronted the king.
David had power, influence, military victories, and a reputation.
But none of those things could turn his wrongdoing into righteousness.
When Nathan exposed him, David said:
“I have sinned against the LORD.” — 2 Samuel 12:13 (KJV)
No elaborate public relations campaign.
No claim that his position made him untouchable.
No attempt to make his victims responsible for his choices.
Just the terrible truth.
I have sinned.
Psalm 51 gives us one of Scripture's most profound expressions of repentance associated with David's sin.
In Psalm 51:10, David cries:
“Create in me a clean heart, O God; and renew a right spirit within me.” (KJV)
The Hebrew begins:
לֵב טָהוֹר בְּרָא־לִי אֱלֹהִים
Lev tahor bera-li Elohim.
“Create for me a clean heart, O God.”
The verb בְּרָא (bera) comes from the Hebrew root ברא (bara), meaning “to create.”
David is not merely asking God to improve his public image.
He is pleading for an inward work that he cannot accomplish through appearances, status, or excuses.
He needs a clean heart.
And so do we.
But do not misunderstand David's story.
God's forgiveness did not eliminate every earthly consequence of David's actions.
The consequences within his household were severe.
Repentance did not make the murdered man return home.
Forgiveness did not make the damage disappear.
That is why genuine repentance is more than feeling terrible after being exposed.
It means turning away from sin, accepting responsibility, making appropriate restitution where possible, and refusing to demand that those we harmed immediately trust us again.
God can forgive a sinner without declaring that the sinner's actions were harmless.
And that is good news, because it means grace is truthful.
It does not require us to lie about the past.
Now consider the marriages of the patriarchs and kings.
Abraham's household experienced deep tension involving Sarah and Hagar.
Jacob's family became entangled in rivalry between Leah and Rachel, alongside relationships with Bilhah and Zilpah.
Solomon's many wives and concubines became part of the spiritual disaster described in 1 Kings 11.
Scripture records polygamy, but the repeated presence of polygamy in biblical narratives does not mean God presents it as His ideal.
From Genesis 2:24, marriage is described through the union of a man and his wife becoming one flesh.
Jesus returns to this creation pattern in Matthew 19:4–6.
The Bible's narratives show how far human households can drift from God's design.
And the consequences are painfully recognizable.
Favoritism.
Competition.
Resentment.
Emotional abandonment.
Children growing up inside adult conflicts they never created.
Families that appear prosperous from the outside while quietly breaking apart within.
Some readers know exactly what that feels like.
You grew up in a house where love felt conditional.
Where adults chose sides.
Where betrayal was never discussed.
Where everyone learned to pretend that nothing was wrong.
And now you are trying to build a healthy marriage without repeating the patterns that wounded you.
Listen carefully.
Your family history can influence you.
But through Christ, it does not have to determine every decision you make.
You may need wise counsel, repentance, boundaries, patient healing, and years of learning healthier ways to love.
Transformation is not always instantaneous.
But the Gospel gives us reason to hope that inherited patterns of sin and dysfunction need not have the final word.
Then there is Joseph.
Genesis 39 tells us that Potiphar's wife repeatedly attempted to seduce him.
Joseph refused.
He recognized that yielding would be a grave sin against God and a betrayal of trust.
When he fled from her advances, she used his abandoned garment to falsely accuse him.
And Joseph was imprisoned.
Think about that.
He did what was right.
And his life became harder.
He resisted temptation.
And suffered injustice.
He honored God.
And found himself behind bars.
Some people desperately need to hear this because they have been taught that obedience always produces immediate comfort.
It doesn't.
Sometimes obedience costs you a relationship.
Sometimes integrity costs you an opportunity.
Sometimes refusing to participate in wrongdoing makes you the target of accusations.
Joseph's story also teaches us to take allegations seriously without abandoning the importance of truth and evidence.
False accusations are real, and so are genuine victims whose reports are unfairly dismissed.
Justice requires careful investigation, not automatic assumptions based on reputation, gender, influence, or public opinion.
And when Joseph's circumstances eventually changed, it was not because the false accusation had suddenly become true or because suffering itself was good.
God was at work even in circumstances shaped by human evil.
Years later, Joseph could tell his brothers:
“Ye thought evil against me; but God meant it unto good.” — Genesis 50:20 (KJV)
Notice what he did not say.
He did not say their evil was actually good.
He distinguished their intentions from God's providential purpose.
That distinction is precious.
Because God can bring redemption out of evil without becoming the author or approver of that evil.
And then we come to a woman surrounded by accusers.
John 8:1–11 tells the familiar account of a woman caught in adultery and brought before Jesus.
There is an important textual detail that deserves honesty.

The passage commonly called the woman caught in adultery, John 7:53–8:11, is absent from many of the earliest surviving Greek manuscripts of John's Gospel. Modern Bible translations often mark it with a textual note.
For that reason, we should not conceal the manuscript question or build a doctrine upon this passage alone.

Yet the account, long received and treasured in Christian tradition, portrays themes consistent with the wider biblical witness: Jesus' opposition to hypocrisy, His mercy toward sinners, and His call to abandon sin.
Picture the scene as the account presents it.
A woman stands publicly accused.
Religious leaders surround her.
They want a verdict.
They want to trap Jesus.
And they seem far more interested in using the woman as a weapon than in pursuing justice.
Where is the man involved?
The narrative does not tell us.
But the omission makes the scene even more troubling, especially since the Mosaic law addressed both parties in adultery.
Jesus does not celebrate adultery.
He does not announce that sin no longer matters.
Instead, He challenges the accusers.
“He that is without sin among you, let him first cast a stone at her.” — John 8:7 (KJV)
One by one, the accusers depart.
And then Jesus speaks words that have brought hope to countless troubled consciences.
“Neither do I condemn thee: go, and sin no more.” — John 8:11 (KJV)
The traditional Greek text reads:
Οὐδὲ ἐγώ σε κατακρίνω· πορεύου, ἀπὸ τοῦ νῦν μηκέτι ἁμάρτανε.
Oude egō se katakrinō; poreuou, apo tou nyn mēketi hamartane.
“Neither do I condemn you; go, and from now on sin no more.”
Notice the two truths held together.
Mercy.
And a call to change.
Not condemnation without hope.
Not acceptance of sin without repentance.
Mercy that opens the door to a different life.
And perhaps that is what someone reading this has been searching for.
Not another person willing to excuse everything.
Not another person eager to expose everything.
But a Savior who knows the truth and calls sinners into the light.
A Savior who does not need to pretend that sin is harmless in order to offer forgiveness.
A Savior who is holy enough to confront what is wrong and merciful enough to welcome the repentant.
And now we reach the words that make this entire conversation impossible to ignore.
Paul writes to the church in Corinth:
He goes on to name various forms of unrighteousness, including sexual immorality, adultery, theft, greed, drunkenness, abusive speech, and exploitation.
These warnings are serious.
Paul is not telling the church that persistent, unrepentant sin is spiritually harmless.
He is warning believers not to confuse belonging to Christ with permission to continue living in rebellion against God.
And then comes one of the most breathtaking turns in the New Testament.
“And such were some of you.” — 1 Corinthians 6:11 (KJV)
Read that again.
Such.
Were.
Some.
Of.
You.
Not because these believers had never committed terrible sins.
Not because their histories had been spotless.
Not because they had earned a second chance through religious performance.
But because something had happened to them through Jesus Christ.
Paul continues:
“But ye are washed, but ye are sanctified, but ye are justified in the name of the Lord Jesus, and by the Spirit of our God.”
The Greek begins:
καὶ ταῦτά τινες ἦτε
Kai tauta tines ēte.
“And such were some of you.”
Then Paul declares:
ἀλλὰ ἀπελούσασθε, ἀλλὰ ἡγιάσθητε, ἀλλὰ ἐδικαιώθητε
Alla apelousasthe, alla hēgiasthēte, alla edikaiōthēte.
“But you were washed, but you were sanctified, but you were justified.”
These are not three flattering compliments.
They describe the decisive change in identity and standing that belongs to those united to Christ.
To be washed points to cleansing from sin.
To be sanctified speaks of being set apart for God.
To be justified speaks of being declared righteous before God.
And Paul makes clear where this saving work comes from.
Not human achievement.
Not a carefully managed reputation.
Not a donation.
In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ and by the Spirit of our God.
This is the Gospel.
The sinner is not saved by pretending to be innocent.
The sinner is saved by the grace of God through Jesus Christ.
The guilty do not purchase forgiveness.
They receive mercy through the crucified and risen Savior.
And those who belong to Christ are called into a new way of life.
But there is another distinction we cannot afford to miss.
A person who has suffered sexual exploitation, assault, or betrayal does not need forgiveness for the sin committed against them.
They need justice, protection, compassion, and healing.
Those who have sinned need repentance.
Those who have been harmed need care.
Some people need both, for different parts of their stories.
And Jesus is not confused about any of it.
He knows what happened.
He knows who chose what.
He knows what was concealed.
He knows which tears came from remorse and which came from being wounded by another person's cruelty.
Nothing is hidden from Him.
That should humble the person who has been protecting a secret sin.
And it should comfort the person whose suffering has been ignored.
Because the same Christ who invites sinners to repent also identifies Himself with the vulnerable and calls His people to love truth, mercy, and justice.
Now think about the cross.
There is no greater exposure of human sin.
Religious hypocrisy.
Political cowardice.
Betrayal.
False testimony.
Violence.
Mockery.
An innocent man condemned.
And at the center stands Jesus Christ.
Not a Savior who committed the scandals He came to redeem.
But the sinless Son of God who willingly gave Himself for sinners.
“For he hath made him to be sin for us, who knew no sin; that we might be made the righteousness of God in him.” — 2 Corinthians 5:21 (KJV)
Jesus did not become morally sinful.
He bore the judgment due to sin as our sinless substitute.
And His resurrection declares that sin and death do not have the final victory.
This is why Christian hope is greater than self-improvement.
It is why repentance is possible without despair.
It is why a person's past does not have to become their permanent spiritual identity.
And it is why no one should confuse the Gospel with a promise that every marriage will be repaired, every criminal consequence removed, or every broken relationship restored.
Some marriages can be healed through genuine repentance, safety, accountability, and patient rebuilding of trust.
Some relationships must end because continuing them would expose people to further harm.
Some wounds require professional counseling and long-term support.
Some injustices require legal intervention.
And sometimes faithful obedience means accepting that reconciliation cannot happen without truth, safety, and meaningful change.
Jesus never promised that following Him would erase every earthly consequence.
He promised something greater than a painless life.
Reconciliation with God.
Forgiveness through His blood.
The gift of His Spirit.
And the hope of eternal life.
So where does that leave you tonight?
Maybe you are the one who betrayed someone's trust.
Stop defending what you know was wrong.
Bring it into the light.
Seek forgiveness from God through Christ, take responsibility, and begin walking in repentance.
Maybe you are the one who was betrayed.
You do not have to pretend the betrayal was insignificant.
You are allowed to grieve.
You are allowed to seek help.
You are allowed to establish boundaries.
And you are not required to rush into trusting someone who has not demonstrated trustworthy change.
Maybe your family is falling apart.
You are exhausted from trying to hold together what other people keep tearing down.
Bring that exhaustion before the Lord.
Ask Him for wisdom, courage, and the right people to help you make faithful decisions.
Maybe you have spent years believing that because your family history was filled with scandal, your future must look the same.
It doesn't have to.
The grace of Jesus Christ is not limited by the sins of your ancestors.
And maybe you are the person who looks completely fine on Sunday.
You know the songs.
You know when to say amen.
You know how to smile when someone asks how you are doing.
But inside, something is collapsing.
You are tired of hiding.
Tired of pretending.
Tired of carrying a secret that is slowly hardening your heart.
Then listen to the invitation of Jesus:
“Come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest.” — Matthew 11:28 (KJV)
Not because sin doesn't matter.
But because Christ is mighty to save.
You can stop pretending that you are beyond the reach of His mercy.
You can stop treating your shame as if it were stronger than His cross.
You can stop assuming that your darkest chapter has already written the ending.
Jesus Christ is still calling sinners to repentance and offering grace to everyone who comes to Him in faith.
Pray.
Not a polished prayer.
Not a performance.
Just tell God the truth.

“Lord Jesus, You know my history. You know what I have done, what has been done to me, and what I have tried to hide. Forgive my sins. Heal what is wounded. Give me courage to face the truth, turn from evil, and walk in Your ways. Teach me to trust Your grace without making excuses for sin. I believe You died for sinners and rose again. Lead me into the life You are calling me to live. Amen.”
If that prayer reflects your heart, don't leave it as a passing emotion.
Open your Bible.
Find a faithful local church where Scripture is taught and people are cared for responsibly.
Seek mature Christian support.
And when serious harm is involved, seek appropriate professional or legal help as well.
Spiritual growth is not meant to happen in isolation.
This is part of why Gospel Warrior exists.
Not to entertain people with religious controversy.
Not to turn another person's pain into content.
But to keep pointing people back to the truth of God's Word and the transforming grace of Jesus Christ.
These resources are intended to help you keep learning long after the emotions of a single article have faded.
Because one powerful moment can awaken the heart.
But faithful discipleship helps shape the life that follows.
It is a voluntary way to help sustain and expand this ministry's work—making biblical teaching, Christian resources, and Gospel-centered encouragement available to more people.
As 2 Corinthians 9:7 teaches:
“God loveth a cheerful giver.” (KJV)
You glorify Him through faith in Christ, obedience to His Word, love for others, generosity, and a life surrendered to His will.
Not because merchandise is the heart of this ministry.
It isn't.
Jesus is.
The resources are tools.
The mission is discipleship.
And the hope is that more people will encounter the truth that Christ saves sinners, confronts evil, restores dignity, and calls His people into transformed lives.
Not because every person needs to know your private story.
Not because public engagement proves spiritual maturity.
But because someone in your circle may be carrying a burden they have never found the courage to explain.
A friend whose marriage is collapsing.
A relative who has quietly walked away from church.
A young person confused about sexuality, shame, and the meaning of grace.
A believer trapped in a cycle of sin and secrecy.
Or a wounded person who desperately needs to understand that God does not blame them for someone else's abuse.
You may never know who reads what you share.
But one truthful message about Jesus can become the beginning of an important conversation.

If someone came to mind while reading, consider tagging them if doing so would encourage rather than embarrass them. You can also send this privately with a simple message: “I thought this might encourage you.”
Return to the Scriptures.
Return to the cross.
Return to the truth.
And before you leave, I want to hear from you.
Not your most polished religious answer.
Not something you think will impress other Christians.
Something real.
You do not owe the internet your trauma, your confession, or your private history. You can also pray silently or reach out to someone trustworthy.
But perhaps your honest words will remind another struggling believer that they are not the only one still learning how to walk in the light.
Because the Gospel is not a story about respectable people proving that they never needed rescue.
It is the announcement that the holy Son of God came to save sinners.
It is the announcement that evil is real, judgment is serious, mercy is available, and repentance matters.
It is the announcement that the cross is sufficient for everyone who comes to Christ in faith.
And that the resurrection has opened a future that human sin could never create.
The Bible did not hide the incest.
It did not hide the exploitation.
It did not hide the adultery.
It did not hide the polygamy, the false accusations, the shattered households, or the painful consequences of human rebellion.
It told the truth.
And then it revealed the One who is the Truth.
Jesus Christ.
The Savior who does not excuse sin.
The Redeemer who does not abandon the repentant.
The righteous Judge who sees the oppressed.
The risen Lord who makes all things new.
And one day, according to Revelation 21:4, God will wipe away every tear, and death, mourning, crying, and pain will be no more.
Until then, we live by faith.
We pursue holiness.
We protect the vulnerable.
We seek justice.
We confess our sins.
We receive grace.
And we keep following Jesus.
Because your worst chapter does not have to be your final chapter.
The world may remember the scandal, but in Christ, the final word belongs neither to your sin nor to the people who wounded you—it belongs to the Savior who gave His life to redeem you.
